title: VII. The First And Rightful Lover
paragraphs: Mitya crossed the room in long, quick strides and went straight to the table.

“Gentlemen,” he said, loudly, almost shouting, yet stumbling over every word, “I ... I’m all right! Don’t be afraid!” he exclaimed. “I—nothing’s the matter,” he said, suddenly turning to Grushenka, who had shrunk back in her chair toward Kalganov and was gripping his hand. “I ... I’m coming, too. I’m here till morning. Gentlemen, may I stay with you till morning? Only till morning, one last time, in this very room?”
He put this last question to the fat little man with the pipe, who sat on the sofa. The man took the pipe from his lips with great dignity and said sternly:
“_Panie_, this is a private party. There are other rooms.”
“Why, it’s Dmitri Fyodorovitch! What’s the matter with you?” Kalganov broke in. “Sit down with us. How are you?”
“Delighted to see you, my dear ... my precious fellow. I always thought the world of you.” Mitya answered joyfully and eagerly, and held out his hand across the table at once.
“Ow! What a grip you have! You’ve nearly broken my fingers,” laughed Kalganov.

“He always grips like that, always,” Grushenka put in cheerfully, with a timid smile. One look at Mitya’s face had suddenly convinced her that he wasn’t going to make a scene. She watched him with keen curiosity, and with some worry still. Something in him struck her. In fact, the last thing she had expected was for him to walk in and talk like this at such a moment.
“Good evening,” Maximov said blandly from the left. Mitya rushed over to him, too.

“Good evening. You’re here, too! I’m so glad to find you here, too! Gentlemen, gentlemen, I—” (He turned again to the Polish gentleman with the pipe, plainly taking him for the most important person there.) “I flew here.... I wanted to spend my last day, my last hour in this room, in this very room ... where I, too, worshiped ... my queen.... Forgive me, _panie_,” he cried wildly, “I flew here and swore— Oh, don’t be afraid, it’s my last night! Let’s drink to a good understanding between us. They’ll bring the wine in a minute.... I brought this along.” (Something made him pull out his bundle of notes.) “Allow me, _panie_! I want music, singing, a revel, just as we had before. But the worm, the useless worm, will crawl away, and there’ll be nothing left of him. On my last night I’ll honor my day of joy.”

He was almost choking. He had so much, so much to say, and nothing came out of his mouth but odd exclamations. The Pole stared hard at him, then at the bundle of notes in his hand, then at Grushenka, and plainly didn’t know what to make of it.
“If my suverin lady is permitting—” he started.

“What’s ‘suverin’? ‘Sovereign,’ I suppose?” Grushenka cut in. “You talk so funny I can’t help laughing. Sit down, Mitya, what are you going on about? Please don’t scare us. You won’t scare us, will you? If you won’t, I’m glad to see you ...”
“Me, scare you?” cried Mitya, flinging up his hands. “Oh, pass me by, go your way, I won’t stand in your road!...”

And suddenly he startled them all, and no doubt himself too. He dropped onto a chair and burst into tears, turning his face to the far wall, his arms wrapped tight around the chair back as though he were hugging it.

“Oh, come now, what a man you are!” cried Grushenka reproachfully. “That’s how he always comes to see me—he starts talking, and I can’t make out what he means. He cried like this once before, and here he is crying again! It’s a disgrace! What are you crying for? _As though you had anything to cry for!_” she added mysteriously, stressing every word, a little irritably.
“I ... I’m not crying.... Well, good evening!” He swung round in his chair at once and laughed—not his abrupt, wooden laugh but a long, shaky, silent, nervous one.

“Well, you’re at it again.... Come on, cheer up, cheer up!” Grushenka coaxed him. “I’m very glad you came, very glad, Mitya, do you hear, I’m very glad! I want him to stay here with us,” she declared to the whole room, though her words were clearly aimed at the man on the sofa. “That’s what I want, that’s what I want! And if he goes, I’m going, too!” she added, her eyes flashing.
“Whatever my queen commands is law!” announced the Pole, kissing Grushenka’s hand with a gallant air. “Please, _panie_, join our company,” he added politely to Mitya.
Mitya sprang up, evidently meaning to launch into another tirade, but no words came.
“Let’s drink, _panie_,” was all he blurted out in place of a speech. Everyone laughed.

“Heavens! I thought he was going to start in again!” Grushenka said nervously. “Listen, Mitya,” she went on, pressing him, “stop prancing about. But it’s nice that you’ve brought champagne. I’d like some myself, and I can’t bear liqueurs. And best of all, you’re here yourself. We were dreadfully bored.... You’ve come on a spree again, I suppose? But put that money away. Where did you get so much?”

The whole time, Mitya had been holding the crumpled bundle of notes in his hand, and every eye in the room was on it, the Poles’ most of all. Embarrassed, he hastily shoved it into his pocket. He blushed. Just then the innkeeper came in with an uncorked bottle of champagne and glasses on a tray. Mitya grabbed the bottle, but he was so rattled that he had no idea what to do with it. Kalganov took it out of his hands and poured the champagne.

“Another! Bring another bottle!” Mitya shouted to the innkeeper. Forgetting to clink glasses with the Pole he had so solemnly asked to drink to their good understanding, he downed his glass without waiting for anyone else. His whole face changed at once. The solemn, tragic look he had walked in with was gone, and something childlike took its place. He seemed suddenly gentle and subdued. He looked around at everyone, shy and happy, with a constant little nervous laugh, and with the blissful look of a dog that has done wrong, been punished and been forgiven. He seemed to have forgotten everything, and he gazed around at them all with a childlike smile of delight. He looked at Grushenka, laughing the whole time, and pulled his chair right up beside hers. Gradually he had begun to form some idea of the two Poles, though he had no clear picture of them yet.

The Pole on the sofa impressed him with his dignified manner and his Polish accent, and most of all with his pipe. “Well, so what? It’s a good thing he smokes a pipe,” he thought. The Pole’s puffy, middle-aged face, with its tiny nose and its two very thin, pointed, dyed, cheeky-looking mustaches, hadn’t raised the slightest suspicion in Mitya so far. He wasn’t even particularly struck by the man’s ridiculous wig, made in Siberia, with love-locks combed foolishly forward over the temples. “It must be all right, since he wears a wig,” he went on, musing blissfully. The other Pole, the younger one, was staring at the company with insolent defiance and listening to the talk in silent contempt. He impressed Mitya only by his great height, which made a striking contrast with the Pole on the sofa. “If he stood up, he’d be six foot three.” The thought flitted through Mitya’s head. It also occurred to him that this man must be the other’s friend, a kind of “bodyguard,” and that the big Pole was no doubt at the service of the little Pole with the pipe. But all this seemed to Mitya perfectly proper and not to be questioned. In his doglike mood of submission, every feeling of rivalry had died out.

He completely failed to understand Grushenka’s mood, or the mysterious tone of some of her words. All he understood, with a thrill in his heart, was that she was being kind to him, that she had forgiven him and let him sit by her. He was beside himself with joy, watching her sip her champagne. The silence in the room seemed to strike him, though, and he looked around at everyone with expectant eyes.
“Why are we just sitting here, gentlemen? Why don’t you get something going?” his smiling eyes seemed to ask.
“He keeps talking nonsense, and we’ve all been laughing,” Kalganov said suddenly, as if he had read Mitya’s thought, and he pointed at Maximov.
Mitya promptly stared at Kalganov, then at Maximov.
“Talking nonsense, is he?” he laughed his short, wooden laugh, suddenly delighted about something—“ha ha!”
“Yes. Believe it or not, he swears that all our cavalry officers in the twenties married Polish women. Isn’t that awful rot?”
“Polish women?” Mitya repeated, in sheer ecstasy.

Kalganov knew very well how Mitya felt about Grushenka, and he had guessed about the Pole as well. But that interested him little, perhaps not at all. What interested him was Maximov. He had come here with Maximov by chance, and he was meeting the Poles at this inn for the first time in his life. He had known Grushenka before and had once visited her with someone, but she hadn’t warmed to him. Tonight, though, she looked at him very fondly. Before Mitya arrived she had been fussing over him, but somehow it didn’t move him. He was a boy, not yet twenty, dressed like a dandy, with a very charming fair-skinned face and splendid thick fair hair. Out of that fair face looked beautiful pale blue eyes, with an intelligent and at times even deep expression, beyond his years in fact, though the young man sometimes looked and talked just like a child, and wasn’t the least ashamed of it, even when he noticed it himself. As a rule he was very willful, even capricious, though always friendly. Now and then there was something fixed and stubborn in his look. He would look at you and listen, and all the while seem to be dreaming doggedly of something else. He was often listless and lazy; at other times he would get excited, sometimes, it seemed, over the most trivial things.

“Just think, I’ve been dragging him around with me for the last four days,” he went on, drawling lazily, quite naturally though, with no affectation at all. “Ever since your brother, remember, shoved him off the carriage and sent him flying. That’s when I took an interest in him, and I took him with me to the country. But he talks such rot that I’m ashamed to be seen with him. I’m taking him back.”
“The gentleman has not seen Polish ladies, and says what is not possible,” the Pole with the pipe told Maximov.
He spoke Russian reasonably well, better, at any rate, than he let on. Whenever he used a Russian word, he twisted it into a Polish shape.
“But I was married to a Polish lady myself,” Maximov tittered.
“But did you serve in the cavalry? You were talking about the cavalry. Were you a cavalry officer?” Kalganov chimed in immediately.
“A cavalry officer, is he? Ha ha!” cried Mitya, listening eagerly, his questioning eyes going from one speaker to the next, as if there were no telling what he might hear from any of them.

“No, you see,” Maximov said, turning to him. “What I mean is, those pretty Polish ladies ... when they danced the mazurka with our Uhlans ... when one of them dances the mazurka with a Uhlan, she jumps onto his knee like a kitten ... a little white one ... and the _pan_-father and _pan_-mother watch and let it happen.... They let it happen ... and the next day the Uhlan comes and proposes.... That’s how it is ... proposes, he he!” Maximov finished, tittering.

“The _pan_ is a _lajdak_!” the tall Pole on the chair suddenly growled, crossing one leg over the other. Mitya’s eye fell on his huge greased boot with its thick, dirty sole. Both Poles’ clothes looked rather greasy.
“Now what’s this, _lajdak_! What’s he scolding about?” said Grushenka, suddenly annoyed.
“_Pani_ Agrippina, the gentleman saw servant girls in Poland, not ladies of good family,” the Pole with the pipe told Grushenka.
“You can count on that,” the tall Pole snapped scornfully.
“What next! Let him talk! People talk, so why stop them? It livens things up,” Grushenka said crossly.
“I’m not stopping them, _pani_,” said the Pole in the wig. He gave Grushenka a long look, sank back into dignified silence, and went on sucking his pipe.

“No, no. The Polish gentleman told the truth.” Kalganov was worked up again, as though it were a question of enormous importance. “He’s never been to Poland, so how can he talk about it? I suppose you weren’t married in Poland, were you?”

“No, in the Province of Smolensk. But a Uhlan had already brought her to Russia before that, my future wife, together with her mamma, her aunt, and another woman relative who had a grown-up son. He brought her straight from Poland and handed her over to me. He was a lieutenant in our regiment, a very nice young man. At first he meant to marry her himself. In the end he didn’t, because she turned out to be lame.”
“So you married a lame woman?” cried Kalganov.
“Yes. The two of them deceived me a little at the time, and kept it hidden. I thought she was hopping; she kept hopping.... I thought it was for fun.”
“She was so happy to be marrying you!” yelled Kalganov in a ringing, childish voice.

“Yes, so happy. But it turned out to be for quite another reason. Later, once we were married, that very evening after the wedding, she confessed, and asked forgiveness in a very touching way. ‘As a child I jumped over a puddle once,’ she said, ‘and hurt my leg.’ He he!”
Kalganov burst into the most childish laughter and nearly fell onto the sofa. Grushenka laughed, too. Mitya was at the peak of happiness.

“You know, that’s the truth, he isn’t lying this time,” Kalganov exclaimed, turning to Mitya; “and you know, he’s been married twice; it’s his first wife he’s talking about. But his second wife, you know, ran away, and she’s alive now.”
“Is that possible?” said Mitya, turning quickly to Maximov, utterly astonished.

“Yes. She did run away. I’ve had that unpleasant experience,” Maximov agreed modestly, “with a _monsieur_. And what made it worse, she’d had all my little property made over to her beforehand. ‘You’re an educated man,’ she told me. ‘You can always make a living.’ With that she settled my affairs. A venerable bishop once said to me: ‘One of your wives was lame, but the other was too light-footed.’ He he!”

“Listen, listen!” cried Kalganov, bubbling over. “If he tells lies—and he often does—he only does it to amuse us all. There’s no harm in that, is there? You know, sometimes I like him. He’s dreadfully low, but it comes naturally to him, eh? Don’t you think so? Some people are low for gain, but he’s simply made that way. Just think, he claims (he argued about it all the way yesterday) that Gogol wrote _Dead Souls_ about him. Remember, there’s a landowner named Maximov in it, the one Nozdryov thrashed. He was charged, remember, ‘with inflicting bodily injury with rods on the landowner Maximov while drunk.’ Can you believe it, he claims he was that Maximov and that he was beaten! Now can that be true? Tchitchikov made his journey at the very latest at the beginning of the twenties, so the dates don’t fit. He couldn’t have been thrashed then, could he?”
It was hard to guess what Kalganov was so stirred up about, but his excitement was real. Mitya went along with him without protest.
“Well, so what if they did thrash him!” he cried, laughing.
“It isn’t that they thrashed me, exactly, but what I mean is—” Maximov put in.
“What do you mean? Either they thrashed you or they didn’t.”
“What o’clock is it, _panie_?” the Pole with the pipe asked his tall friend, looking bored. The other shrugged in answer. Neither of them had a watch.

“Why not talk? Let other people talk. Are other people not allowed to talk just because you’re bored?” Grushenka flew at him, obviously set on picking a quarrel. Something seemed to dawn on Mitya’s mind for the first time. This time the Pole answered with unmistakable irritation.
“_Pani_, I raised no objection. I said nothing.”
“Fine, then. Come, tell us your story,” Grushenka called to Maximov. “Why is everyone so quiet?”

“There’s nothing to tell, it’s all so silly,” Maximov answered at once, plainly pleased, with a little mincing air. “Besides, it’s all allegory in Gogol, because he gave every name a meaning. Nozdryov was really called Nosov, and Kuvshinikov had quite a different name, Shkvornev. Fenardi really was called Fenardi, only he wasn’t an Italian but a Russian. And Mamsel Fenardi was a pretty girl, with her pretty little legs in tights and a short little skirt with spangles, and she kept turning round and round, only not for four hours but for four minutes, and she bewitched everyone...”
“But what did they beat you for?” cried Kalganov.
“For Piron!” Maximov answered.
“What Piron?” cried Mitya.

“The famous French writer Piron. We were all drinking, a big party of us, in a tavern at that same fair. They had invited me, and first of all I started quoting epigrams. ‘Is that you, Boileau? What a funny outfit!’ and Boileau replies that he’s off to a masquerade, meaning the baths, he he! They took it as aimed at them, so I hurried to recite another, a very biting one, known to every educated person:
Yes, Sappho and Phaon are we! But one grief is weighing on me. You don’t know your way to the sea!

That offended them even more, and they began to abuse me in the most unseemly way. And as bad luck would have it, to smooth things over I started telling a very cultured anecdote about Piron, how he was refused entry to the French Academy and, to get his revenge, wrote his own epitaph:
Ci-gît Piron qui ne fut rien, Pas même académicien.
They grabbed me and thrashed me.”
“But what for? What for?”
“For my education. A man can be thrashed for anything,” Maximov concluded, briefly and sententiously.
“Oh, stop it! That’s all stupid, I don’t want to listen. I thought it would be fun,” Grushenka snapped at them suddenly.

Mitya flinched and stopped laughing at once. The tall Pole stood up. He looked bored and out of place, and with a haughty air he began pacing from corner to corner of the room, hands clasped behind his back.
“Ah, he can’t sit still,” said Grushenka, eyeing him with scorn. Mitya began to feel uneasy. He also noticed that the Pole on the sofa kept looking at him with irritation.
“_Panie!_” cried Mitya. “Come, let’s drink! You and the other _pan_, too! Let’s all drink.”
In a flash he had dragged three glasses over and filled them with champagne.
“To Poland, _panovie_! I drink to your Poland!” cried Mitya.
“With great pleasure, _panie_,” said the Pole on the sofa, with dignity and a friendly, lordly air, and he picked up his glass.
“And the other _pan_, what’s his name? Drink, most illustrious, take your glass!” Mitya urged.
“Pan Vrublevsky,” put in the Pole on the sofa.
Pan Vrublevsky came over to the table, rolling a little as he walked.
“To Poland, _panovie!_” cried Mitya, lifting his glass. “Hurrah!”
All three drank. Mitya grabbed the bottle and filled three glasses again.
“Now to Russia, _panovie_, and let’s be brothers!”
“Pour some for us,” said Grushenka. “I’ll drink to Russia, too!”
“So will I,” said Kalganov.
“And I will, too ... to Russia, the old grandmother!” tittered Maximov.
“Everybody! Everybody!” cried Mitya. “Trifon Borissovitch, bring more bottles!”
The other three bottles Mitya had brought with him were set on the table. Mitya filled the glasses.
“To Russia! Hurrah!” he shouted again. Everyone drank the toast except the Poles, and Grushenka downed her whole glass in one go. The Poles left theirs untouched.
“What’s this, _panovie_?” cried Mitya. “Won’t you drink?”
Pan Vrublevsky took his glass, raised it and said in a ringing voice:
“To Russia as she was before 1772.”
“Now that’s more like it!” cried the other Pole, and they both emptied their glasses at once.
“You’re fools, you _panovie_,” Mitya blurted out suddenly.
“_Panie!_” shouted both Poles in a threatening way, bristling at Mitya like a pair of fighting cocks. Pan Vrublevsky was the angrier of the two.
“Can a man help loving his own country?” he shouted.

“Quiet! No quarreling! I won’t have it!” cried Grushenka in a commanding voice, and she stamped her foot on the floor. Her face was flushed and her eyes were bright. The glass she had just drunk was clearly working on her. Mitya was badly frightened.
“_Panovie_, forgive me! It was my fault, I’m sorry. Vrublevsky, _panie_ Vrublevsky, I’m sorry.”
“You, anyway, shut your mouth! Sit down, you idiot!” Grushenka scolded, angry and annoyed.
They all sat down. Nobody spoke; they just looked at one another.
“Gentlemen, it was all my fault,” Mitya began again, unable to make sense of Grushenka’s words. “Well, why are we just sitting here? What can we do ... to have some fun again?”
“Ach, nothing here is fun at all!” Kalganov mumbled lazily.
“Let’s play faro again, like we did a while ago,” Maximov tittered suddenly.
“Faro? Splendid!” cried Mitya. “If only the _panovie_—”
“It’s lite, _panovie_,” the Pole on the sofa answered, as though reluctantly.
“True,” agreed Pan Vrublevsky.
“Lite? What’s that, ‘lite’?” asked Grushenka.
“Late, _pani_! I mean ‘a late hour,’” the Pole on the sofa explained.

“With them it’s always late. They can never do anything!” Grushenka almost shrieked in her anger. “They’re dull themselves, so they want everyone else dull, too. Before you came, Mitya, they sat here just as silent and kept turning up their noses at me.”
“My goddess!” cried the Pole on the sofa. “I see you’re not kindly toward me, and that is why I’m gloomy. I’m ready, _panie_,” he added, turning to Mitya.
“Go ahead, _panie_,” Mitya agreed. He pulled his notes out of his pocket and put two hundred-rouble notes on the table. “I want to lose a lot to you. Take your cards. Deal the bank.”
“We’ll take the cards from the landlord, _panie_,” said the little Pole, gravely and firmly.
“That’s much the best way,” chimed in Pan Vrublevsky.
“From the landlord? Fine, I see, we’ll get them from him. Cards!” Mitya shouted to the landlord.

The landlord brought a new pack, still sealed. He told Mitya that the girls were getting ready and the Jews with the cymbals would probably arrive soon, but the cart with the provisions had not come yet. Mitya jumped up from the table and ran into the next room to give instructions. Only three girls had turned up, though, and Marya wasn’t there yet. And he himself didn’t know what instructions to give, or why he had run out. All he did was tell them to unpack the presents for the girls from the box, the sweets, the toffee and the fondants. “And vodka for Andrey, vodka for Andrey!” he cried in a hurry. “I was rude to Andrey!”
Suddenly Maximov, who had followed him out, tapped him on the shoulder.
“Give me five roubles,” he whispered to Mitya. “I’ll put something on faro, too, he he!”
“Capital! Splendid! Take ten, here!”
Again he pulled all the notes out of his pocket and picked out a ten-rouble one. “And if you lose that, come back, come back.”

“Very good,” Maximov whispered joyfully, and scurried back. Mitya went back too, apologizing for keeping them waiting. The Poles had sat down and opened the pack. They looked far friendlier now, almost warm. The Pole on the sofa had lit another pipe and was getting ready to deal. He had a solemn look about him.
“Take your places, gentlemen,” cried Pan Vrublevsky.
“No, I won’t play any more,” said Kalganov. “I just lost fifty roubles to them.”
“The _pan_ had no luck. Maybe he’ll be lucky this time,” the Pole on the sofa said, turning to him.
“How much is in the bank? Enough to match me?” asked Mitya.
“It depends, _panie_. A hundred, maybe two hundred, as much as you care to stake.”
“A million!” laughed Mitya.
“Perhaps the Pan Captain has heard of Pan Podvysotsky?”
“What Podvysotsky?”

“In Warsaw there was a bank, and anyone at all could come and bet against it. Podvysotsky comes, sees a thousand gold pieces, bets against the bank. The banker says, ‘_Panie_ Podvysotsky, are you putting down the gold, or are we to trust your honor?’ ‘My honor, _panie_,’ says Podvysotsky. ‘So much the better.’ The banker throws the dice. Podvysotsky wins. ‘Take it, _panie_,’ says the banker, and he pulls out the drawer and gives him a million. ‘Take it, _panie_, this is what you won.’ There was a million in the bank. ‘I didn’t know that,’ says Podvysotsky. ‘_Panie_ Podvysotsky,’ said the banker, ‘you pledged your honor and we pledged ours.’ Podvysotsky took the million.”
“That’s not true,” said Kalganov.
“_Panie_ Kalganov, in gentlemen’s company one does not say such things.”

“As if a Polish gambler would hand over a million!” cried Mitya, but he checked himself at once. “Forgive me, _panie_, my fault again. He would, he would hand over a million, for honor, for Polish honor. See how well I speak Polish, ha ha! Here, I bet ten roubles, the knave leads.”

“And I put one rouble on the queen, the queen of hearts, the pretty little _panienotchka_, he he!” laughed Maximov. He drew out his queen and, as though trying to hide it from everybody, edged right up close and crossed himself quickly under the table. Mitya won. The rouble won, too.
“A corner!” cried Mitya.
“I’ll bet one more rouble, a ‘single’ stake,” Maximov muttered gleefully, enormously pleased at having won a rouble.
“Lost!” shouted Mitya. “A ‘double’ on the seven!”
The seven was beaten as well.
“Stop!” cried Kalganov suddenly.
“Double! Double!” Mitya doubled his stakes, and every time he doubled a card, the Poles beat it. The rouble stakes kept winning.
“Double again!” shouted Mitya furiously.
“You have lost two hundred, _panie_. Will you stake another hundred?” the Pole on the sofa asked.
“What? Two hundred gone already? Then two hundred more! All doubles!”
And pulling the money from his pocket, Mitya was about to throw two hundred roubles down on the queen, but Kalganov covered it with his hand.
“Enough!” he shouted in his ringing voice.
“What’s the matter with you?” Mitya stared at him.
“Enough! I don’t want you playing any more. Don’t!”
“Why?”
“Because I don’t want it. Blast it, come away. That’s why. I won’t let you keep playing.”
Mitya looked at him in amazement.
“Give it up, Mitya. Maybe he’s right. You’ve lost plenty already,” said Grushenka, with a curious note in her voice. Both Poles stood up, looking deeply offended.
“Are you joking, _panie_?” said the short man, giving Kalganov a stern look.
“How dare you!” Pan Vrublevsky growled at Kalganov, too.
“Don’t you dare shout like that,” cried Grushenka. “Ah, you turkey-cocks!”
Mitya looked from one to the other. But something in Grushenka’s face suddenly caught his attention, and in that same instant a new idea flashed into his head—a strange new idea!
“_Pani_ Agrippina,” the little Pole was starting, red with anger, when Mitya suddenly stepped up to him and clapped him on the shoulder.
“Most illustrious, a word with you.”
“What do you want?”
“In the next room. I have two words to tell you, something pleasant, very pleasant. You’ll be glad to hear it.”
The little _pan_ was startled and gave Mitya a wary look. Still, he agreed straight away, on condition that Pan Vrublevsky went with them.
“The bodyguard? Let him come, I want him, too. I must have him!” cried Mitya. “March, _panovie_!”
“Where are you going?” asked Grushenka, anxious.
“We’ll be back in a moment,” Mitya answered.
There was a kind of daring in his eyes, a sudden confidence. His face had looked very different when he came into the room an hour before.

He led the Poles not to the big room where the chorus of girls was gathering and the table was being laid, but to the bedroom on the right. The trunks and packages were kept there, and there were two large beds, each with a heap of cotton pillows piled up like a pyramid. A candle was burning on a small deal table in the corner. The little man and Mitya sat down at this table across from each other, while the huge Vrublevsky stood by them with his hands behind his back. The Poles looked stern but plainly wanted to know what was coming.
“What can I do for you, _panie_?” lisped the little Pole.
“Well, look here, _panie_, I won’t keep you long. Here’s money for you,” and he took out his notes. “Do you want three thousand? Take it and be on your way.”
The Pole stared at Mitya, wide-eyed, with a probing look.
“Three thousand, _panie_?” He exchanged a glance with Vrublevsky.

“Three, _panovie_, three! Listen, _panie_, I can see you’re a sensible man. Take the three thousand and go to the devil, and take Vrublevsky with you—do you hear? But at once, this very minute, and for good. You understand, _panie_, for good. There’s the door, go out through it. What have you got there, a greatcoat, a fur coat? I’ll bring it out to you. They’ll bring the horses round straight away, and then—good-by, _panie_!”
Mitya waited for an answer, sure of himself. He had no doubts at all. A look of extraordinary determination came over the Pole’s face.
“And the money, _panie_?”

“The money, _panie_? Five hundred roubles I’ll give you this very moment for the journey, as a first payment, and two thousand five hundred tomorrow in town—I swear on my honor, I’ll get it, I’ll get it at any price!” cried Mitya.
The Poles exchanged glances again. The short man’s face grew more forbidding.

“Seven hundred, seven hundred, not five hundred, right now, this minute, cash in hand!” Mitya added, sensing that something was wrong. “What’s the matter, _panie_? Don’t you trust me? I can’t hand over the whole three thousand all at once. If I did, you might come back to her tomorrow.... Besides, I haven’t got the three thousand on me. It’s at home in town,” faltered Mitya, his heart sinking with every word. “On my word, the money is there, hidden away.”
In an instant a remarkable sense of his own dignity appeared on the little man’s face.
“What next?” he asked sarcastically. “For shame!” and he spat on the floor. Pan Vrublevsky spat too.
“You’re doing that, _panie_,” said Mitya, seeing with despair that it was all over, “because you hope to get more out of Grushenka? You’re a pair of capons, that’s what you are!”

“This is a mortal insult!” The little Pole went red as a crab and walked out of the room briskly, as if he couldn’t bear to hear another word. Vrublevsky lumbered out after him, and Mitya followed, confused and crushed. He was afraid of Grushenka, afraid the _pan_ would start shouting right away. And so he did. The Pole came into the room and flung himself down before Grushenka in a theatrical pose.
“_Pani_ Agrippina, I have suffered a mortal insult!” he exclaimed. But Grushenka suddenly lost all patience, as though they had hurt her in her most tender spot.
“Speak Russian! Speak Russian!” she cried. “Not another word of Polish! You used to speak Russian. You can’t have forgotten it in five years.”
She was red with fury.
“_Pani_ Agrippina—”
“My name is Agrafena, Grushenka. Speak Russian or I won’t listen!”
The Pole gasped with offended dignity and quickly and pompously said in broken Russian:
“_Pani_ Agrafena, I came here to forget the past and forgive it, to forget all that happened up to today—”
“Forgive? You came here to forgive me?” Grushenka cut him off, leaping up from her seat.

“Exactly so, _pani_. I am not pusillanimous, I am magnanimous. But I was astounded when I saw your lovers. Pan Mitya offered me three thousand, in the other room, to go away. I spat in the _pan’s_ face.”
“What? He offered you money for me?” cried Grushenka, hysterical. “Is that true, Mitya? How dare you? Am I for sale?”
“_Panie, panie!_” yelled Mitya. “She’s pure and shining, and I have never been her lover! That’s a lie....”

“How dare you stand up for me to him?” shrieked Grushenka. “It wasn’t virtue that kept me pure, and it wasn’t fear of Kuzma. I did it so I could hold my head up when I met him, and call him a scoundrel to his face. And did he really turn down the money?”
“He took it! He took it!” cried Mitya. “Only he wanted all three thousand at once, and I could give him just seven hundred on the spot.”
“I see: he heard I had money, and came here to marry me!”
“_Pani_ Agrippina!” cried the little Pole. “I am—a knight, I am—a nobleman, and not a _lajdak_. I came here to make you my wife, and I find you a different woman, perverse and shameless.”

“Oh, go back where you came from! I’ll tell them to throw you out, and out you’ll go,” cried Grushenka, furious. “What a fool I’ve been, a fool, to be so miserable these five years! And it wasn’t even for his sake, it was my own anger that made me miserable. And this isn’t he at all! Was he like this? This could be his father! Where did you get that wig? He was a falcon, and this is a gander. He used to laugh and sing for me.... And I’ve been crying for five years, damned fool that I was, wretched and shameless!”
She sank back into her low chair and hid her face in her hands. At that moment the Mokroe chorus began to sing in the room on the left—a rollicking dance song.
“A regular Sodom!” Vrublevsky roared suddenly. “Landlord, drive those shameless hussies out!”
The landlord had been peering curiously in at the door for some time. Now he heard the shouting and guessed that his guests were quarreling, and he came into the room at once.
“What are you yelling for? Do you want to burst your throat?” he said to Vrublevsky, with astonishing rudeness.
“Animal!” bellowed Pan Vrublevsky.

“Animal? And what kind of cards were you playing with just now? I gave you a pack and you hid it. You played with marked cards! I could send you to Siberia for playing with false cards, do you know that? It’s the same as forging banknotes....”
And going over to the sofa, he stuck his fingers between the back and the cushion and pulled out a sealed pack of cards.
“Here’s my pack, still sealed!”
He held it up and showed it to everyone in the room. “From where I stood I saw him slip my pack away and put his own in its place—you’re a cheat and no gentleman!”
“And I saw the _pan_ switch a card twice!” cried Kalganov.
“How shameful! How shameful!” exclaimed Grushenka, wringing her hands and blushing with real shame. “Good Lord, he’s sunk to this!”
“I thought so, too!” said Mitya. But before he had finished saying it, Vrublevsky, his face confused and furious, shook his fist at Grushenka and shouted:
“You low harlot!”
Mitya was on him at once. He seized him with both hands, lifted him off the floor, and in a moment had carried him into the room on the right, the one they had just left.
“I’ve put him down on the floor in there,” he announced, coming straight back, panting with excitement. “He’s struggling, the scoundrel! But he won’t come back, never fear!...”
He shut one half of the folding doors and, holding the other half open a crack, called out to the little Pole:
“Most illustrious, would you care to go out as well?”
“My dear Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” said Trifon Borissovitch, “make them give back the money you lost. It’s as good as stolen from you.”
“I don’t want my fifty roubles back,” Kalganov declared suddenly.
“And I don’t want my two hundred, either,” cried Mitya. “I wouldn’t take it for anything! Let him keep it as a consolation.”
“Bravo, Mitya! You’re a prince, Mitya!” cried Grushenka, and there was a note of fierce anger in her cry.
The little _pan_, red with fury but still careful of his dignity, was heading for the door. He stopped short, though, and said suddenly to Grushenka:
“_Pani_, if you want to come with me, come. If not, good-by.”

And swollen with indignation and self-importance, he went to the door. He was a man of character: he thought so highly of himself that even after all that had happened he still expected her to marry him. Mitya slammed the door behind him.
“Lock it,” said Kalganov. But the key clicked on the other side; they had locked it from inside.
“That’s perfect!” exclaimed Grushenka without mercy. “It serves them right!”
